title: A famous chart drawn by dice
hook: People guess their own rank at random. What does the chart of their guesses look like?

knows: the popular claim that the least skilled are the most overconfident
doesNotKnow: that self-estimates with no link to skill at all already produce the famous chart
so the chart alone can't prove the effect

misconception: The Dunning-Kruger chart shows that the least skilled are uniquely blind to their own lack of skill.
objective: The learner can explain that if self-estimates are pure noise, grouping people by real score makes the bottom quarter's average guess sit near the middle (about the 50th percentile), drawing the classic chart; that guesses matching skill make the lines meet; and that this shows the chart cannot by itself prove the effect, which is contested.

claims.text: In this model, with guesses that are pure noise, the bottom quarter's average guess is about the 50th percentile (49 for seed 42) while its real average is 12.5; with guesses that match skill, the two lines coincide.
claims.source: Demo.tsx simulate(): 1,000 people with real percentiles (i + 0.5)/10, guesses uniform 0-100 from mulberry32(seed). Seed 42 quarter means: real 12.5/37.5/62.5/87.5, guessed 49.2/50.7/52.3/51.5; seeds 43 and 44 give bottom 51.8 and 50.1 (node, 2026-10-14). Seed 42 is the brief's check seed and was not chosen for its result (pattern disclose-chosen-seeds). Expected value is exactly 50 by construction. company/domains/briefs/checks/big-ideas-cycle1-check.mjs #4.

claims.text: Adding a better-than-average shift (+15 in the model) lifts every guess, so the bottom quarter looks even more overconfident.
claims.source: Demo.tsx with shift +15, seed 42: tracking 0 bottom 63.3; tracking 0.3 bottom 53.2 vs real 12.5, top 76.2 vs 87.5; tracking 1 bottom 27.5 (node, 2026-10-14). The +15 and the 0 / 0.3 / 1 tracking levels are the lesson's model, labelled on the stage, not estimates from data.

claims.text: Kruger and Dunning's 1999 chart had this shape: the bottom quarter's self-estimates sat far above its real percentile, and the top quarter's slightly below.
claims.source: Kruger, J. & Dunning, D. (1999), 'Unskilled and unaware of it: how difficulties in recognizing one's own incompetence lead to inflated self-assessments', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 77(6), 1121-1134 (Figure 1 and others; bottom quartile near the 12th percentile estimating around the 60th; figures to confirm). Not opened by the builder.

claims.text: Random-number simulations reproduce the pattern, and some analyses argue that the effect is mostly a statistical artefact.
claims.source: Nuhfer, E. et al. (2016), 'Random number simulations reveal how random noise affects the measurements and graphical portrayals of self-assessed competency', Numeracy 9(1), art. 4; Gignac, G. E. & Zajenkowski, M. (2020), 'The Dunning-Kruger effect is (mostly) a statistical artefact: valid approaches to testing the hypothesis with individual differences data', Intelligence 80, 101449. Not opened by the builder.

claims.text: Where it stops: noise drawing the shape does not prove there is no effect; other analyses find a smaller real effect, so the question is not settled.
claims.source: Jansen, R. A., Rafferty, A. N. & Griffiths, T. L. (2021), 'A rational model of the Dunning-Kruger effect supports insensitivity to evidence in low performers', Nature Human Behaviour 5, 756-763 (to confirm). Flag for the fact-checker: charter rule, contested ideas name both sides; c4 is the artefact side, this is the real-effect side. Not opened by the builder.

recall.question: A study groups drivers by real skill and finds the worst quarter rate themselves about average. What should you check before concluding they are uniquely deluded?
options: Whether random guesses would also average out near the middle
Whether the worst drivers had more accidents
recall.why: If self-ratings were pure noise, every group would average near the middle, so the worst group would look overconfident by construction. The chart needs a test beyond its shape.
